rationale: B wins by a nose because it is more useful before outreach: it keeps forcing the ugly distinction between savings Ramp found and dollars customers actually acted on. A's "Ramp is giving away the audit and charging for the workflow — the enterprise tier is the real business" is a decent idea dressed as a conclusion; B's "How much of that figure was actually cancelled or renegotiated after finance approval, versus flagged and left alone?" is the question that saves the founder from getting exposed by the first finance reporter. B still needs one headline defanged, but its proof discipline is sharper.
gaps_in_A: "Ramp is giving away the audit and charging for the workflow — the enterprise tier is the real business" overstates the pricing and revenue strategy; the update says an enterprise tier is coming, not that workflow monetization is confirmed.
"The auto-renewal, long the SaaS vendor's quiet profit center, now has a bot reading the fine print" invents contract-reading behavior and implies vendor economics the supplied facts do not prove.
"a meaningful share of SaaS revenue is renewal inertia and seats nobody logs into" needs outside evidence; as written it treats a market claim as if it came with the update.
A never cleanly centers the reporter-killing gap between identified savings and realized savings; "How much of the 'savings' is recurring versus one-time?" is adjacent, but not sharp enough.
gaps_in_B: "The AI agent's biggest savings didn't come from negotiating. They came from cancelling." is too definite; the update says mostly unused seats and auto-renewals, not cancellation versus negotiation outcomes.
"the 200-company beta is the first public dataset behind it" adds "first public" without support.
"regulated back-office functions" overstates the supplied facts; finance approvals are sensitive, but no regulated-function claim was given.
"Ramp gives away software-spend auditing for free, and plans to charge enterprises later" assumes the enterprise tier is paid; plausible, but not stated.
